newsitem.title: UK: Gasoline to play scrooge for European motorists.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline to play scrooge for European motorists.

text.p: European motorists hitting the road during the holidays will be greeted by sharply higher gasoline prices that will force them to dig deeper into their pockets to fill up their tanks.

Robust international prices for crude oil and gasoline, another round of tax increases in some countries and a stronger dollar against many local currencies will make pump prices more expensive than a year ago, industry analysts said.
"In national currency terms there has been a double increase in some countries," said Peter Regnier, director of Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
"The effect of strong international prices reinforced by the depreciation of national currencies against the dollar means that where prices have not moved up, they will inevitably do so," he said.
"Happy Christmas to all your readers," he said.
World oil prices are valued in dollars.

Strong demand from the U.S. that has sucked gasoline supplies out of Europe, and a strike at three Elf refineries in France this month also tightened inventories and boosted wholesale prices by nearly 75 percent from a year ago.
Retail prices before taxes, which vary greatly among countries, showed 10 pct increases.
"What we're finding is that the U.S. is becoming increasingly import dependent and mopping up the surplus in Europe," said Keith Hamm, chairman of Petroleum Economics Ltd in London.
"Going into the early part of next year the U.S. is likely to be as concerned as much about gasoline as it is about heating oil now," he said.
Crude and home heating oil prices in the U.S. and Europe rose to their highest levels since the Gulf War this autumn, dragging up gasoline as well.
Refiners scrambling to replenish heating oil inventories may have done so at the expense of gasoline, putting this market in the spotlight when the winter focus is normally on heating oil.
"It's like robbing Peter to pay Paul," Hamm said. "I spent 30 pounds ($49.28) filling my car on Saturday and I don't think I've ever paid that much."

Britain, as expected, increased the petrol tax on November 26 by three pence per litre and some analysts said the ferocious retail price war was showing signs of loosening, at least for the time being.
British retail prices have risen 2.3 pence per litre in the last two weeks, so the tax increased has not fully hit, Regnier said.
British prices still remain among the cheapest in Europe, even though taxes make up more than 75 percent of its cost.
OPAL provided the following average unleaded pump price per litre before taxes in Europe for major brands last week, and the year-ago levels, in local currency terms:
Belgium 35.80 32.00
Denmark 6.33 5.71
France 6.19 5.77
Germany 1.669 1.549
Netherlands 2.01 1.87
